title: The empty circle
hookLine: picture eight: both ox and herder forgotten, an empty circle (Ox-Herding 8)
tomorrow: after the empty circle, why paint a river and flowers?

cards: A blank page can feel like a threat, or like the best page in the sketchbook. Kuoan's eighth picture is blank: one circle, nothing inside. Ox gone, herder gone.
And his verse ends on a strange line: here are the footprints of the old masters. Which masters? One of them, the story goes, was a kitchen worker who couldn't read.

teach.b: The Platform Sutra tells it. The Zen teacher Hongren told his monks to write a verse showing what they understood; the one who truly saw would receive his robe.
His head monk, Shenxiu, wrote his on a hallway wall at night: the body is the bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it clean always, and let no dust land.
Everyone admired it, and Hongren had the monks recite it.
Out in the rice-pounding shed worked Huineng, who couldn't read. He had first heard a sutra recited while selling firewood in a market, and walked a long way to find this teacher.

He asked someone to read him the verse, then had his own written beside it. In the version told here: bodhi has no tree, the bright mirror has no stand; from the beginning, not one thing exists; where could dust land?

teach.h: THE ROBE GOES TO THE KITCHEN.
teach.b: Hongren passed the robe to Huineng, at night, and sent him away for his safety.
That's the teaching of the empty circle, as Huineng's heirs told it; the Platform Sutra comes from his side, and Shenxiu was honored in his own day as a great teacher.
In this telling, awakening isn't a mirror you keep polished; there was never a thing there to polish.
Kuoan's verse says it with fire: how could a snowflake last in a red-hot furnace?
Whip, rope, herder, ox, all gone into emptiness. Not a void. Open.

how: Zen communities tell Huineng's story from the Platform Sutra, and Zen painters draw the enso, a circle in one stroke. People on this path let one practice be empty of anything to achieve.

s: Kuoan's eighth picture is an empty circle
whip, rope, herder and ox: all gone into emptiness.
in the Platform Sutra, the head monk's verse wins the robe
Huineng, a rice-pounding worker who couldn't read, received it.
emptiness in Zen means nothing matters
the popular misreading. Kuoan's circle is open, not a void: nothing fixed to cling to.

games.q: your roommate treats meditation as scrubbing her mind clean of every bad thought, and feels like she's failing. which verse speaks to her?
o: Huineng's: there's no mirror to keep spotless; from the beginning, not one thing.
Shenxiu's, read harder: scrub more often, and the dust will finally stop.
neither: she should stop sitting until her thoughts are already clean.
games.why: Shenxiu's mirror verse was admired, but Hongren gave the robe to Huineng, whose verse says there's no stand and no mirror: nothing there for dust to land on.

practice: Take a pen and draw one circle, in a single stroke, without fixing it. Zen painters call this an enso. Let it come out however it comes out.
Then sit with it for the two minutes: nothing inside, nothing missing.

wordCard.voice: The empty circle: Kuoan's eighth picture. Ox and herder both forgotten; from the beginning, not one thing.

orig.note: Chinese: from the beginning, not one thing; Huineng's line in the Platform Sutra.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the empty circle, open rather than empty-handed. Picture eight, and the page is blank on purpose.
